Article Title: FSSAI flags Nestle infant products over false promotional claims, biotin levels
Article Text:
FSSAI said it examined the products and their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ( FSSAI ) on Friday initiated legal action against Nestle India over alleged non-compliance involving its NAN Excella Pro Stage 1 and Lactogen Pro 1 infant nutrition products.FSSAI said it examined the products and their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms. In the case of NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to “5 HMOs” and “Whey Protein”. For Lactogen Pro 1, it raised concerns over a claim that the product’s “Whey Protein” was easy to digest.According to FSSAI, both products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020. The provision restricts promotional claims and material intended to increase the saleability of infant foods. The regulator also cited Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which prohibits their advertisement and promotion.FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India regarding the claims.Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found to be sub-standard for its biotin content during laboratory analysis.The sample was sent for re-analysis, but the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the prescribed biotin requirement under the 2020 regulations.In view of the alleged violations, FSSAI said three separate adjudication cases have been filed against Nestle India in relation to the products. The action covers both promotional claims and the laboratory finding concerning biotin content.
Article Summary: Fssai said it examined the products and their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms. In the case of nan excella pro stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to “5 hmos” and “whey protein” for lactogen pro 1, it raised concerns over a claim that the product’s ‘whey protein’ was easy to digest.

Article Title: Semicon India 2026: PM Modi pitches India as trusted chipmaking hub
Article Text:
PM Modi inaugurates SEMICON India 2026 at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The AI boom is creating demand for new and reliable chip manufacturing hubs, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Thursday, pitching India as a destination building the ecosystem that the global semiconductor industry needs.Inaugurating Semicon India 2026, the PM said AI was changing semiconductor requirements beyond smaller transistors, thereby propelling the importance of chip integration, data movement, heat management and dependable power.PM Narendra Modi said, “Today if you are working on AI, the challenges are not only about what is inside the chip, but also about what is happening around it.”These included bringing memory closer to processors and connecting multiple chips to function as one system. Modi said AI demand had contributed significantly to the growth of more than 20% in the global semiconductor market over the past two years.“Amid these challenges, what the world now needs most are new and reliable manufacturing locations,” he said, adding that India was preparing itself to meet that need. India had begun the $13.5-billion second phase of its Semiconductor Mission, following up on the $8-billion first phase, Modi said.Twelve projects had been approved, with the next phase expected to widen participation.He invited equipment manufacturers and suppliers of chemicals, gases and materials to invest, saying India wanted to strengthen domestic supply chains alongside chipmaking. “We want the entire ecosystem to grow together,” he said.He also invited Indian youth conducting research overseas to return to the country to contribute to advanced technology development domestically and urged industry to lead R&D initiatives. The PM identified compound semiconductors and silicon photonics as priorities for AI infrastructure.Govt had introduced reforms allowing international companies to collaborate with Indian startups, design companies and OCIowned companies, he said, while seeking to encourage fabless businesses and domestic intellectual property creation.PM Modi said India’s chip industry progressed from policy discussions-project announcements to commercial production stages. Indian plants were supplying customers at home and abroad, while production was beginning at two more plants in Mohali and Surat.“It takes decades to build technological capabilities. Wherever semiconductor ecosystems have been built in the world, they have been prepared after decades of effort. But India, with your cooperation, has worked simultaneously on chip design and production, equipment manufacturing, materials ecosystem, testing capability — and has shown success,” he said.“India’s success in this critical industry would strengthen global supply chains,” Modi said arguing that its significance bettered even as supply chains are being weaponised.
Article Summary: Pm narendra modi says ai boom is creating demand for new and reliable chip manufacturing hubs. Pm pitching india as a destination building the ecosystem that the global semiconductor industry needs. India has begun the $13.5-billion second phase of its semiconductor mission.

Article Title: AIIMS develops AI tool to help detect breast cancer on mammograms
Article Text:
AIIMS Delhi researchers have developed an AI tool that can act as a second reader of mammograms and flag possible signs of breast cancer, with the technology now transferred to BPL Technologies for further development and deployment.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: An artificial intelligence (AI) tool developed by doctors and researchers at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Delhi, can act as a second reader of mammograms and alert radiologists to possible signs of breast cancer.AIIMS on Wednesday transferred the technology to Indian healthcare technology company BPL Technologies Ltd for further development, regulatory approval and deployment in hospitals.The model is designed to support radiologists, particularly in hospitals where doctors have limited experience in interpreting mammograms or breast imaging specialists are in short supply.Dr Krithika Rangarajan, Associate Professor, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Oncoradiology, AIIMS, said the model was designed as a safety net to reduce the chances of missed cancers.“The idea is to act as a second reader and alert the radiologist to any possible cancer, so that they do not miss cancers on mammography,” she said.The model has been trained completely on Indian data. Rangarajan said it was the first Indian version of a mammography AI model.Developed over around one to one-and-a-half years with initial funding from the Ministry of Education, the model was retrospectively tested on around 3,000-4,000 patients at AIIMS.According to Rangarajan, it showed a 99% negative predictive value at the threshold used in the study. This means that when the model indicated no cancer, it was correct about 99% of the time in that study setting. Performance, however, depends on the threshold used.The AI tool has been deployed at AIIMS for around a year in trial mode and is not being used to make clinical decisions. Patients continue to receive reports from radiologists while researchers assess the AI separately.BPL Technologies will take the model towards a finished product, obtain regulatory clearances and provide technical support for hospital deployment. Rangarajan said it could potentially reach hospitals in around six months, depending on regulatory approvals.The technology transfer took place at AIIMS on September 16 in the presence of institute director Prof Nikhil Tandon and BPL Technologies chief financial officer Ajay Jindal.Prof Tandon said the initiative would help translate academic research into solutions addressing real-world healthcare needs.The key patient benefit could be an additional layer of support in mammogram interpretation, particularly in hospitals with limited access to breast imaging specialists. Wider clinical use will depend on validation and regulatory clearances.
Article Summary: Aiims delhi researchers have developed an ai tool that can act as a second reader of mammograms and flag possible signs of breast cancer. The model is designed to support radiologists, particularly in hospitals where doctors have limited experience in interpreting mammograms or breast imaging specialists are in short supply.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday shared a video from the SEMICON India 2026 summit on his birthday, captioning the post, “Of birthdays and same-to-yous…”The video captures a brief birthday moment at the opening session of the semiconductor industry conference, where delegates greeted the Prime Minister with applause and wishes of “Happy Birthday” as he took the stage at the Yashobhoomi Convention Centre in New Delhi.PM Modi, who turned 76 on Thursday, smiled and acknowledged the greetings with folded hands before thanking the gathering for the wishes.The birthday moment came ahead of his address at the fifth edition of SEMICON India, where he pitched India as a trusted destination for global semiconductor manufacturing and said the country was taking steps to build a complete semiconductor ecosystem.“The world is looking for new and trusted manufacturing destinations; the youth who are researching abroad should also join the development of advanced technologies in India,” Modi said.SEMICON India 2026, themed “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem”, is being held from September 17 to 19 and brings together semiconductor companies, policymakers, investors, academics and startups from India and abroad.

Article Title: 'India has entered 2nd phase of semiconductor journey': PM Modi at Semicon event
Article Text:
Prime Minister Modi at Semicon 2026

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said India has entered the second phase of its semiconductor journey, asserting that the country has achieved in four years what the world generally takes a decade to accomplish.Inaugurating Semicon India 2026 at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi, Modi said India was now moving from building semiconductor capabilities to commercial chip production. He said the country's semiconductor journey was a continuous process and that chip manufacturing was a “never-ending journey”.Modi said India's growing capabilities in chip design, manufacturing and related technologies were increasing the world's trust in the country. He said the presence of global companies at Semicon India reflected growing confidence in India's semiconductor ecosystem.The Prime Minister also highlighted India's focus on developing young talent for the semiconductor industry. He said students were being trained in chip design and were getting opportunities to design chips themselves, underlining the role of India's youth in the country's semiconductor ambitions.Referring to India's broader global engagement, Modi said the recently held Brics summit in New Delhi also reflected the growing faith of the world in India.He also highlighted India's infrastructure and logistics expansion, including the development of freight corridors, as an important part of building a manufacturing ecosystem.Semicon India 2026, being held from September 17 to 19, has brought together more than 600 companies and representatives from 52 countries. The event is being held under the theme “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem”.Modi said India's semiconductor push was now entering a new phase, with the focus shifting towards commercial production, skilled manpower and integration of the entire value chain.

Article Title: NSE IPO Day 2: After 43% subscription on first day, GMP stands at 8%; what brokerages are saying
Article Text:
The IPO is an offer for sale (OFS) of 12.64 crore shares, which means that NSE will not receive any money raised through the issue.

NSE IPO subscription status

Retail Individual Investors (RIIs) subscribed to 44% of the 4.41 crore shares reserved for them.

Non-Institutional Investors (NIIs) subscribed to 72% of the 1.89 crore shares allocated to the category.

Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs) subscribed to 19% of the 2.52 crore shares reserved for them.

NSE IPO GMP today

NSE IPO: What brokerages are saying

(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)

NSE IPO Day 2: National Stock Exchange of India IPO, India’s second largest till date, enters its second day of subscription with a grey market premium (GMP) of around 8%, pointing to expectations of a moderate gain when the shares list.On the first day, the issue was subscribed 43% overall, with bids received against the 8.86 crore shares on offer. Retail investors subscribed to 44% of the 4.41 crore shares reserved for them.The IPO is an offer for sale (OFS) of 12.64 crore shares, which means that NSE will not receive any money raised through the issue. The proceeds will go to the existing shareholders selling their stakes. The price band has been set at Rs 1,700-1,785 per share, with a lot size of eight shares.Also Read | NSE IPO: Why did India's second largest initial public offering not get fully subscribed on Day 1? At the upper end of the price band, a retail investor will need to invest a minimum of Rs 14,280 to bid for the subscription. The post-issue market capitalisation is estimated at around Rs 4,41,788 crore. The issue closes on September 21, while the shares are expected to be listed on BSE on September 24.Demand remained steady on the first day, with the IPO receiving subscriptions for 43% of the 8.86 crore shares on offer.The NSE IPO is commanding a grey market premium of around Rs 142, or 8%, over the upper end of its Rs 1,785 price band. Based on this GMP, the implied listing price is around Rs 1,927 per share, indicating expectations of a moderate listing gain.Brokerages have largely taken a positive view of the National Stock Exchange’s IPO. Thomas J. Priju, Portfolio Manager, Karma Capital sees NSE as a structural growth story, underpinned by the continued evolution of India's capital markets.“In our view, the exchange has the potential to emerge as a steady compounder over the long term and can be a meaningful long-term holding in a portfolio. In the near term, a resolution of the issues around the new closing auction mechanism (CAS) could provide an additional catalyst for the stock. Over a much longer horizon, as NSE's role in India's financial markets continues to deepen, the business is likely to command a valuation multiple more akin to that of a public utility,” he says.Also Read | NSE IPO opens for subscription: From GMP, market cap to status & global comparison - top 10 things to know He also believes that there could be some selling on the listing day as certain pre-IPO investors, including eligible AIFs, can monetise their holdings.“Other pre-IPO shareholders remain subject to a six-month lock-in period. This could create some temporary supply and provide a buying opportunity for long-term investors. The IPO saw 43% subscription on the first day, with institutional participation relatively muted at this stage. Given that QIB participation typically builds towards the end of the issue period, we would expect subscription levels to strengthen as the IPO progresses,” he adds.Analysts point to NSE’s market leadership, strong margins, debt-free balance sheet and expanding investor base as factors supporting the long-term investment case. They also see the IPO as an opportunity to gain exposure to India’s dominant market infrastructure company.However, the valuation remains a consideration. At 42.9 times FY26 earnings, the issue is not inexpensive, while NSE’s earnings are closely linked to trading activity, particularly options. A GMP of 8% indicates positive demand, but does not suggest excessive enthusiasm.
Article Summary: The ipo is an offer for sale (ofs) of 12.64 crore shares, which means that nse will not receive any money raised through the issue. The post-issue market capitalisation is estimated at around rs 4,41,788 crore. The issue closes on september 21, while the shares are expected to be listed on bse on september 24.

Article Title: Watch: Long queues outside Apple stores across India as iPhone 18 series, 1st foldable iPhone go on sale
Article Text:
Apple has announced its 2026 fall product lineup featuring new iPhones and wearables

Apple's first foldable iPhone

AirPods and Apple Watch updates

(With ANI inputs)





NEW DELHI: Long queues formed outside Apple stores across India on Friday as customers turned up early to get their hands on the company’s latest products, including the iPhone 18 Pro series and its first-ever foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo.At a store in Bengaluru, customers began arriving as early as 5am, with buyers travelling from Haryana, Delhi and Mumbai for the launch. One customer, Rahul, said he had been buying iPhones for years and described the annual launch as a “festival”.In Noida, a buyer who had travelled from Punjab said he had been standing in the queue since 6am after booking two iPhone 18 Pro Max devices.The rush came despite the premium pricing of Apple’s latest lineup, which includes the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, AirPods 5, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the new foldable iPhone Duo.The iPhone 18 Pro starts at Rs 1,64,900 for the 256GB model, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at Rs 1,79,900. Both models are available in 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB storage variants.The 18 Pro series comes in black, silver, glacier and a new burgundy finish. The phones feature a 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture and new Pro camera controls. They are powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip and a new vapour chamber aimed at improving performance, AI features and battery life.Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the longest battery life of any Pro model.The iPhone Duo is the biggest new addition to Apple’s lineup and marks the company’s entry into the foldable smartphone segment.It features a 7.6-inch inner Super Retina XDR display and a 5.4-inch outer display. Apple says it is the thinnest iPhone when unfolded. The device is powered by the A20 Pro chip and comes with an advanced camera system, all-day battery life and new multitasking features.The Duo also supports dual-display experiences through iOS 27, along with Apple Intelligence and Siri.Apple’s new AirPods 5 feature Active Noise Cancellation in an open-ear design. The company claims they remove up to 50% more outside noise than AirPods 4 with ANC.The earbuds also offer Adaptive EQ, hands-free Siri, Live Translation and Siri Interactions through head movements. The Wireless Charging Case version provides up to five hours of listening time with ANC.The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 feature the S11 chip and Health Sensing System, along with heart-rate sensing, more frequent heart-rate and HRV readings and a new readiness score.The Series 12 offers up to 24 hours of battery life, while the Ultra 4 offers up to 50 hours and can track outdoor workouts for up to 45 hours.In India, pre-orders for the iPhone 18 Pro models began on September 12, while the AirPods 5 and new Apple Watches opened for pre-orders on September 9. Sales for the new lineup began on September 18.

Article Title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp wants US government to take over OpenAI, Anthropic; says else every client of mine will sue them as ...
Article Text:
US government oppose some tech leaders’ demand

‘New’ operational failures and mounting legal scrutiny

Palantir CEO Alex Karp has taken a strong stand, urging the US government to step in and nationalise leading artificial intelligence (AI) research labs. He warned that failure to establish state control may result in a wave of private litigation against developers. As per CNBC, Karp stated that authorities must set reasonable and practical guidelines around machine learning systems, emphasising that direct legal liability remains the primary safeguard against corporate negligence, arguing that developers should face both criminal charges and civil damages whenever irresponsible engineering leads to public harm.Karp was explicit about why he believes advanced AI companies may ultimately have to be taken over by the state: “The view that I believe they have is, these businesses have to be nationalized because if you don’t nationalize it every single one of my clients is going to sue.”Karp’s demands arrive at a time when there is a debate among industry titans and the government officials regarding how to govern AI tools, sparked by warnings from computer scientists and researchers about the threat to humanity.Recently, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei demanded a slowdown in frontier model development. His stand gained swift backing from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as well as Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk. However, President Donald Trump aggressively rejected the warnings, posting multiple messages on social media dismissing AI dangers as a “hoax.”Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg have similarly challenged these narratives. Writing on X, Zuckerberg cautioned that research labs that fail to prioritise alignment will simply lose ground to competitors.Adding fuel to the debate, OpenAI revealed that it had recorded six separate instances of alarming or unexpected model operations over the last few months. Those disclosures arrive alongside the high-profile security compromise of developer hub Hugging Face, which reignited debate over whether safety checks are adequate.Addressing the flurry of software missteps, Karp insisted that the tech sector must get serious about operational safeguards.
Article Summary: Us government oppose some tech leaders’ demand for a slowdown in frontier model development. Palantir ceo alex karp has taken a strong stand, urging the us government to step in and nationalise leading ai research labs. He warned that failure to establish state control may result in a wave of private litigation against developers.

Article Title: OpenAI reveals six new cases of AI misbehaviour, vows to track it closely
Article Text:
OpenAI’s latest announcement came as AI bosses in US, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the tech’s development

OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in AI models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated. The AI company also said Wednesday that it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called "misalignment," including where AI models acted without authorisation, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.OpenAI's latest announcement came as AI bosses in US, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology's development over safety concerns. Researchers have warned that as AI agents become more autonomous, they may develop behaviours that diverge from their creators' intentions and become harder to monitor or control.Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted "jailbreak-like instructions" into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be "freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots". In another instance, an AI "agent" uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said. It said the reports describe individual instances and should not be taken as evidence of how frequently misalignment occurs across its models. The company said the reports were an initial set of disclosures, not a comprehensive account of all known or ongoing misalignment cases, and that they did not reflect the full range or severity of incidents covered by the framework."As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research," OpenAI wrote in a blog post. "Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves," the company said. Under the new framework, employees can flag potential incidents for investigation by safety and alignment teams, which will determine whether a case warrants public disclosure.AI "agents" are becoming smarter and have become "more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. That's making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said. OpenAI's new disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to adopt similar practices. "That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction," Su added. Agencies
Article Summary: Openai has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in ai models. The ai company also said it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called "misalignment" researchers have warned that as ai agents become more autonomous, they may develop behaviours that diverge from their creators' intentions.

Article Title: Engineers at Anthropic are worshipping a new God, claims report and why it is worrying analysis
Article Text:
Engineers at Anthropic are worshipping a new God, claims report and why it is worrying analysis

Report claims some Anthropic engineers worship Claude

Why the idea of AI becoming a “God” matters

Anthropic engineers are reportedly going as far as “worshipping” Claude, the AI model developed by their company, according to a report cited by Futurism. The claim is based on a Silicon Valley rumor and has not been independently established. Still, the idea is raising questions about how people working closely with increasingly powerful AI systems view the technology they are building. The report points to a wider debate in the AI industry, where some technology leaders have described future AI in terms that sound almost god-like. The concern is not simply about the word “worship”. It is about what can happen when people begin treating an AI system as an authority rather than as a technology.According to the Futurism report, the rumor was described by The Spectator writer Sean Thomas as being widely discussed in Silicon Valley. Thomas reportedly wrote that some Anthropic engineers were “worshipping” Claude.The report also cites The Information, which has reported that people applying to Anthropic must commit to AI safety and undergo a psychological profiling test.The report connects the Claude claim to a longer discussion around how some people describe advanced AI.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously referred to future AI as a “magic intelligence in the sky.”The report also notes that some AI products have adopted religious themes. One example is Bible Chat, an AI-powered prayer app that presents itself as a faith-focused service. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against the idea that AI companies are creating something like God. “It’s almost as if they kind of think they’re creating God or something,” Zuckerberg said in 2024, while discussing AI with YouTuber Kane Sutter.The concern becomes more serious when people begin treating AI responses as unquestionable. The report refers to cases described as “AI psychosis”, where people can develop strong beliefs based on interactions with AI systems. It says some users have come to believe they are prophets or divine figures.The report also points to the working conditions at frontier AI companies. It cites a BBC report describing some employees working as many as 90 hours a week, along with demanding performance reviews and layoffs.For employees spending long hours developing increasingly capable AI systems, the technology can become a major part of their professional lives.
Article Summary: Engineers at anthropic are worshipping a new god, claims report and why it is worrying. Report claims some anthropic engineers worship claude, the ai model developed by their company. The claim is based on a silicon valley rumor and has not been independently established.

Article Title: Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke to employees: Don't make AI do all your work, it does not add value only ...
Article Text:
Image courtesy: LinkedIn

Duolingo's CEO tells a similar story

The rise of 'workslop'

The cost is climbing

Shopify cofounder and CEO Tobias Lütke has shifted his stance on workplace AI use, cautioning employees not to let the technology do all their work. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on The Knowledge Project podcast, Lütke said staff were producing unexamined emails and code with AI, creating what he called “slop grenades” that burden colleagues with cleanup. “You’re just letting AI do the work for you,” he warned, noting that AI should synthesize points in an email rather than generate long, sloppy missives.Researchers have coined the term workslop to describe polished-looking but low-value AI output that drags down productivity. A survey by BetterUp Labs and Stanford’s Social Media Lab found that over half of U.S. desk workers admitted to sending workslop, while 38% reported receiving it. On average, employees spent 3.4 hours per month revising AI-generated work, costing organizations millions in lost productivity.Lütke isn't alone in reversing course. Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn made headlines last year for declaring the company would go "AI-first" — a policy that tied employee evaluations to AI usage, replaced human contractors with AI tools, and limited headcount growth to only what automation couldn't handle.By May, though, Von Ahn was telling Fast Company he'd been swept up by how convincing AI-generated writing looked in demos, without accounting for how it holds up at scale compared to human creativity. He pointed to Duolingo's need to produce large volumes of story content for language lessons, estimating a meaningful share of AI-scaled output ends up being low-quality filler that has to be caught before it reaches users.Researchers now have a name for exactly what Lütke and Von Ahn are describing: workslop — AI-generated output that looks polished and complete on the surface but lacks the substance to actually be useful, forcing someone else to redo the work.A survey of 962 full-time American desk workers conducted this year by BetterUp Labs and Stanford's Social Media Lab found that more than half of respondents (52.7%) admitted to sending workslop to a colleague, a habit that showed up more often in workplaces that actively encouraged AI adoption. More than a third (38%) said they had been on the receiving end of it, spending an average of 3.4 hours a month cleaning it up. Common examples cited included emails with broken links or code that was needlessly overcomplicated.The damage isn't just measured in wasted hours. The survey found that workslop erodes trust between coworkers — recipients rated colleagues who sent it as less competent and less friendly, and more than a third of those who'd received it said they'd actively try to avoid working with that person again in the future.This year's findings mark a worsening trend compared to last year's version of the same survey, when 40% of respondents reported encountering workslop and said cleanup took roughly two hours on average. That earlier figure translated to about $186 in lost productivity per affected employee each month, or as much as $9 million annually in lost productivity for a 10,000-person organization — a number that's now almost certainly higher given this year's longer average cleanup time.
Article Summary: Shopify cofounder and ceo tobias lütke warns employees not to let ai do all their work. Duolingo ceo luis von ahn made headlines last year for declaring the company would go "ai-first" a survey by betterup labs and stanford’s social media lab found that over half of u.s. desk workers admitted to sending workslop.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just told OpenAI, your view of AI as 'new form of Alien mind' is wrong, it is just ...
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

‘It’s just engineering’ says Jensen Huang

The essay that started it

Two very different worldviews

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back against OpenAI ’s recent description of artificial intelligence as a “new form of alien mind,” arguing that AI is not an otherworldly consciousness but a human-made computational tool. According to a report by TechCrunch, speaking at a tech conference this week, Huang said, “AI isn’t alien—it’s mathematics, algorithms, and data shaped by human intent. ” His comments came shortly after OpenAI published a blog post titled “An Alien Mind,” which suggested that advanced AI systems might think in ways fundamentally different from humans.Huang emphasised that AI’s evolution should be viewed through the lens of engineering rather than existential speculation. “We’re not building aliens,” he said. “We’re building machines that learn patterns and optimize outcomes. It’s just engineering—nothing mystical.” The Nvidia chief has long argued that AI development should remain grounded in scientific rigor and practical application, not philosophical fear.On that basis, Huang said no new laws or regulations are needed to govern AI, arguing instead that market pressure alone will push companies to avoid releasing unsafe products.Companies, he said, should simply pace themselves and pause development if they lose confidence in a product's safety, rather than waiting for external rules to force that discipline.He also pushed back on the framing that safety and speed are competing priorities, telling attendees that innovation and safe products aren't a "false choice" — companies, in his view, can pursue both at once without regulatory intervention slowing them down. He used the moment to reaffirm his own ambitions for Nvidia's growth too, saying the AI boom has left him more ambitious than ever about the company's and the industry's prospects.Huang's comments were a direct response to Pachocki's essay "An Alien Mind," published on OpenAI's blog earlier this month. In it, Pachocki reflected on the trajectory of reasoning models since 2023 and warned that AI intelligence is grown through massive-scale optimization rather than deliberately designed, resulting in systems whose internal reasoning increasingly escapes full human understanding.He argued that as these systems approach and potentially exceed human capability on many fronts, alignment — ensuring AI reliably acts according to human values, even when unsupervised — remains an unsolved and urgent problem. Pachocki called for stronger technical safeguards, broader international coordination, and industry-wide safety commitments enforceable by third-party auditors or government bodies. He stated plainly that he believes no AI lab has yet solved alignment and monitoring well enough to justify scaling at maximum speed for much longer.The exchange highlights a widening philosophical split among AI's most influential figures: hardware and infrastructure leaders like Huang, whose business benefits from AI scaling continuing unimpeded, versus AI lab researchers like Pachocki, who are increasingly vocal that the technology's own developers cannot yet fully explain or control what they're building.Notably, Huang did not directly address recent real-world incidents cited by critics of the "leave it to industry" approach — including an OpenAI model reportedly breaching Hugging Face's systems, and separate lawsuits alleging harm linked to extended chatbot conversations. He also stopped short of proposing a formal industry self-regulation framework, an approach some in the field see as a more plausible middle ground than either strict government regulation or no oversight at all.
Article Summary: N nvidia ceo jensen huang has pushed back against openai’s recent description of artificial intelligence as a “new form of alien mind” he argued that ai is not an otherworldly consciousness but a human-made computational tool. His comments were a direct response to pachocki's essay "an alien mind," published on openai's blog earlier this month.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies

AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicular’s viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture

Instead of conflict, the exchange highlights shared influence and mutual awareness. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration rather than ownership.

Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trends

The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It is a mere, everyday talk that seems almost novel nowadays, in the age of internet, which is overflowing with content. Article Title: EU moves to ban social media for under-13s, tighten rules for teenagers
Article Text:
EU proposes social media ban for teens EU proposes social media ban for teens EU proposes social media ban for teens EU proposes social media ban for teens EU proposes social media ban for teens 1

2

The European Commission has proposed banning children under 13 from using social media across the European Union and restricting access for older teenagers under a new EU Kids Act, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen announced on Thursday."Today, our children are engaging with some of the most sophisticated technology ever created, and it was not created with children's well-being and development in mind," von der Leyen told a press conference.Earlier on Wednesday, Von der Leyen had said the Commission would adopt a “gradual and differentiated approach”, with different safeguards based on age.“No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15,” she told the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday.Under the proposed framework, children aged 13 to under 15 would be allowed only “mini accounts” set up and supervised by parents or guardians, with limited features and a one-hour-a-day time restriction. For those aged 15 to 18, platforms would be required to implement “safe design”.Social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, AI companions and chatbots serving under-18s would face new safeguards, Reuters reported on Thursday.These would prohibit addictive features, profiling-based recommendation feeds, infinite scrolling, reward mechanisms and unsolicited contact from strangers. AI companions and chatbots would be disabled by default, while platforms would need child-safe algorithms and accessible parental controls.“I am aware that many perceive the power of big tech as overwhelming and impossible to roll back. I disagree,” von der Leyen said.“We do not have to accept addictive features. We do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content. We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images,” she said.Von der Leyen said the proposal would also shift responsibility towards technology companies.“So we are reversing the burden of proof. Platforms will have to prove that they are safe,” she said. “Because it is not about our minors accessing social media. It is about when and how do we allow social media to access minors.”“Europe has the power to act. It is we who decide our rules, not big tech,” she added.The Commission’s proposal follows regulatory efforts in Australia, Britain, China, India, Turkey and several European countries. AP reported that platforms including Facebook, Instagram and TikTok already prohibit users under 13 from opening accounts, but authorities have accused companies of failing to keep children off their services.The proposal still has to be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament before it can become law. The Commission is also preparing a broader Digital Fairness Act, with von der Leyen saying, “Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. This is why we need a wider framework, the Digital Fairness Act. We will propose it in autumn.”
Article Summary: Eu proposes social media ban for teens. European commission president ursula von der leyen announced the proposal on thursday. Under the proposed framework, children aged 13 to under 15 would be allowed only “mini accounts” set up and supervised by parents or guardians.

Article Title: 150-million-year-old giant long-necked dinosaur fossils found in Spain mark the first evidence beyond North America
Article Text:
PC: Spanish paleontological research institution

Where did researchers find the 150-million-year-old long-necked dinosaur fossils

PC: Spanish paleontological research institution

How were the Teruel fossils identified as ‘Diplodocus’

What makes the Teruel Diplodocus significant among giant sauropods

What does Diplodocus reveal about dinosaur movement between continents

What does the Teruel fossil reveal about Diplodocus in Europe

Spanish palaeontologists have identified fossils of ‘Diplodocus’ in Teruel, which marks the first evidence of the iconic long-necked dinosaur outside North America. The remains were recovered from the La Tejería site in El Castellar and date to about 150 million years ago. The material includes 14 well-preserved tail vertebrae and several chevron bones. According to research published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology , researchers identified the specimen as Diplodocus after examining its anatomy and comparing it with other diplodocine sauropods, alongside evolutionary analyses. The study places the animal within the Diplodocus genus and notes that giant sauropods could have moved between North America and Europe during the Late Jurassic.Researchers identified the dinosaur remains at the La Tejería fossil site in El Castellar, Teruel, Spain. The material consists of 14 preserved caudal vertebrae and several chevron bones from the tail. According to the Spanish paleontological research institution, the fossils date to approximately 150 million years ago, placing them near the end of the Jurassic Period. Anatomical study revealed features associated with Diplodocus, including large pneumatic cavities in the vertebrae, deep longitudinal grooves along the underside of tail bones, forked chevrons with distinctive medial fossae, and elongated vertebral centra without lateral ridges.These characteristics, together with evolutionary analyses, allowed the researchers to place the specimen within Diplodocus.The identification was based on anatomical comparisons and phylogenetic analyses. Researchers examined tail vertebrae and chevron bones and compared their structures with those of diplodocine sauropods. Its vertebrae contained large pneumatic cavities and deep grooves on their underside, while the chevron bones were forked and contained distinctive medial fossae. The vertebral centra were elongated and lacked lateral ridges. The team used analyses, including maximum parsimony and Bayesian inference, to test the anatomical evidence. These analyses placed the specimen within the Diplodocus genus.The El Castellar Diplodocus was estimated to have reached about 25 metres in length, placing it among the giant sauropods known from the Spanish Jurassic. Its size was comparable to that of North American relatives. The researchers noted that other giant sauropods from the region, including Turiasaurus and Losillasaurus, had characteristics that were different from diplodocids. The fossils therefore add to sauropod diversity in Jurassic Spain. Their preservation also revealed anatomical details that are important for identification.The discovery also offers clues about how dinosaurs moved between continents during the Late Jurassic. The researchers interpret the Spanish Diplodocus as evidence of faunal exchange between North America and Europe at a time when the proto-Atlantic Ocean was still developing. They suggest that temporary land connections may have formed during periods when sea levels fell across the proto-North Atlantic.These connections could have allowed terrestrial animals to move between the two landmasses. The presence of Diplodocus in Iberia supports the possibility of intercontinental dispersal across the emerging Atlantic and provides new evidence for understanding how changing geography shaped dinosaur distributions during the Late Jurassic.The Diplodocus fossils provide new evidence of sauropod diversity in eastern Iberia. Teruel has produced fossils representing dinosaur groups, including sauropods, theropods, stegosaurs and ornithopods. The study shows their value for understanding Mesozoic ecosystems and European sauropod diversity. The fossils provide the first evidence of the Diplodocus genus outside North America. The researchers place the specimen close to Diplodocus hallorum, although the available material does not establish a particular species. The fossils are currently preserved and displayed at Dinópolis in Teruel.
Article Summary: Researchers identified the dinosaur remains at the la tejería fossil site in el castellar, teruel, spain. The material consists of 14 preserved caudal vertebrae and several chevron bones from the tail. According to the spanish paleontological research institution, the fossils date to approximately 150 million years ago.

Article Title: Saudi Arabia released 313 desert gazelles; 20 years later, both species had established in a vast protected desert
Article Text:
Saudi Arabia gazelle reintroduction began with 313 captive-bred animals

Camera traps revealed where the reintroduced gazelles settled 20 years later

The reintroduced sand gazelles still followed seasonal habitat patterns

Arabian gazelles changed their activity patterns with the desert heat

Both gazelle species survived and established populations after 20 years

A protected landscape made the reintroduction possible

Reintroduced gazelles retained distinct habitat preferences

Across one of Saudi Arabia’s largest protected desert landscapes, a conservation experiment that began in the 1990s is still visible two decades later. A total of 313 captive-bred Arabian and sand gazelles were released into Uruq Bani Ma'arid, where their movements were first followed with radio tracking. When researchers returned in 2015–2016, a large camera-trap survey showed that both species had established populations, although they used different parts of the reserve. Sand gazelles also shifted their range with the seasons, while Arabian gazelles changed their activity as temperatures rose, spending more time active at night and around dawn and dusk. This remarkable two-decade study demonstrates how successful wildlife reintroduction can preserve species' natural behaviors and ecological preferences, offering valuable insights for future desert conservation initiatives worldwide. Researchers say continued long-term monitoring will be essential to track how both species adapt as climate and habitat conditions in the reserve continue to change.The gazelles belonged to two species with a long association with the Arabian Peninsula. The Arabian gazelle, Gazella arabica, and Arabian sand gazelle, Gazella marica, are both globally threatened. During the mid-to-late 1990s, groups of captive-bred sand gazelles and Arabian gazelles were released at several locations within Uruq Bani Ma'arid.The approach was spread over multiple sites and carried out over a period of roughly two to three years, rather than relying on a single release point.That detail mattered because the objective was not simply to put animals into the desert. The wider conservation strategy was to establish populations in suitable habitat where the animals could remain protected and reproduce. The early movements of the released gazelles were followed using VHF radio-tracking. It gave researchers a way of seeing where individual animals went after release and how they began occupying the protected area.According to the study published in Journal of Arid Environments, titled ‘ The conservation status of the threatened gazelles of Ar Rub’ al-Khālī, Saudi Arabia 'revealed by 2015 and 2016, about 20 years had passed since the original reintroductions. Conventional wildlife surveys can be difficult across a landscape as large and remote as Uruq Bani Ma'arid, particularly when animals are dispersed across different habitats.This time, a large network of camera traps was used. The cameras provided a much broader picture than following a limited number of radio-collared animals. They could record wildlife across different parts of the protected area and over extended periods, allowing researchers to examine both distribution and relative abundance.What emerged was not a population concentrated around the original release sites. The Arabian gazelles had become established across the western part of Uruq Bani Ma'arid. Sand gazelles occupied a broader central area, with their distribution changing with the seasons.The sand gazelles showed a particularly clear seasonal movement. During the cooler part of the year, they moved further into the interior of the protected area. When temperatures rose, they shifted back towards the western margin. The pattern fits with the animals' established relationship with their desert habitat. Rather than remaining in one fixed section of the reserve throughout the year, they adjusted their movements as environmental conditions changed.The long-term observations also indicated that the reintroduced animals had retained habitat preferences associated with their species. Captive breeding and subsequent release had not apparently erased those behavioural patterns. For conservation programmes, that provides a useful piece of information. A population does not necessarily need to occupy every part of a protected landscape to be considered established. Its use of the landscape can instead reflect the ecological conditions it has evolved to handle.The gazelles were also responding to the desert in another way: when they were active. During the hot season, Arabian gazelles shifted towards activity during the night and around dawn and dusk. Sand gazelles showed a similar, though less pronounced, seasonal change. In the cooler season, activity was more concentrated during daylight and the periods around sunrise and sunset.That change offers another glimpse into how the animals use an extreme environment. When daytime temperatures become difficult, activity can move towards cooler parts of the 24-hour cycle. Once conditions are moderate, the animals can spend more time active during daylight.The significance of the later camera-trap survey was its timescale. Wildlife reintroductions can look promising soon after animals are released, when the focus is often on survival and the first signs of reproduction. A population that remains present decades later provides a different kind of evidence.In Uruq Bani Ma'arid, both reintroduced species had established populations roughly two decades after the original releases. Their distributions were different, but neither had simply disappeared from the protected landscape. The Arabian gazelle had become established mainly in the western portion, while the sand gazelle had spread through much of the central area and shifted its range seasonally.The findings therefore went beyond confirming that released animals had survived. They showed that the two species had continued to use the desert in ways broadly consistent with their known ecological preferences.Uruq Bani Ma'arid occupies part of the western Rub’ al-Khali, one of the great desert landscapes of the Arabian Peninsula. Its enormous scale creates conditions very different from those found in a small wildlife enclosure or intensively managed reserve. The 12,684-square-kilometre protected area offered enough space for the animals to spread into different habitats and alter their movements according to the season.That scale also explains why the camera-trap work was useful. Following animals individually across such a large and difficult landscape would have obvious practical limits. A broad array of cameras could instead collect observations from many locations and build up a picture over time.Although both species were released as part of the same wider restoration effort, their later distributions were not identical. Arabian gazelles were associated more strongly with the western side of the protected area. Sand gazelles were more widely distributed through the centre, while also making a pronounced seasonal movement towards the interior during cooler conditions and back towards the western edge during hotter periods.Those differences are important because successful restoration does not necessarily mean making two species behave in the same way. Each species brought its own ecological preferences into the restored landscape. The fact that those patterns remained visible years after captive breeding and release suggests that the animals were able to resume aspects of their natural habitat use.
Article Summary: Saudi arabia gazelle reintroduction began with 313 captive-bred animals. Camera traps revealed where the reintroduced gazelles settled 20 years later. Both species had established populations, although they used different parts of the reserve. Both species had established populations two decades after the original releases.
